chunks: And from him, from his father, from Muhammad ibn Abdillah ibn Ja'far al-Himyari, who said:

I wrote to the Faqih (peace be upon him) asking him: Is it permissible for a man to perform tasbih (glorification) with the clay of the grave of al-Husayn (peace be upon him), and is there merit in it? He answered, and I read the Tawqi' (autograph reply) and copied from it: 'He performs tasbih with it. There is nothing in tasbih superior to it. And from its merit is that the one who performs tasbih forgets the tasbih (due to absorption), and he rotates the subhah (prayer beads), so that tasbih is recorded for him.'

key_terms.السُّبْحَةَ: Subhah (prayer beads used for counting dhikr)
key_terms.الْفَقِيهِ: The Jurist (a title for the Imam during the Minor Occultation)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling and spiritual merit of using the clay of Imam al-Husayn's grave for prayer beads (tasbih)?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights the Shia practice of using the clay (turrah) of Imam al-Husayn’s grave for dhikr, a tradition rooted in the belief that the earth of the Imams carries spiritual barakah. The Faqih’s response emphasizes the quality of presence (khushu) over mechanical repetition, noting that deep devotion leads to the forgetting of the counting process while the reward remains fully recorded. This underscores the Shia scholarly view that physical objects associated with the Ahl al-Bayt serve as conduits for spiritual elevation and divine grace.
